questions.q: In the recommended layout, why does tempdb ideally sit on the fastest available storage?
options: It has the highest I/O churn of any component, with objects constantly created and dropped and no durability requirement
Because tempdb requires RAID 5 specifically
Because tempdb is the largest file on most servers
Because tempdb never needs to grow, so fast storage is wasted elsewhere
questions.explain: tempdb sees extremely high write churn from temp objects, spills, and version stores, making fast storage especially valuable there.

questions.q: What is the performance reason for separating data and log onto different drives?
options: Data's random I/O and the log's sequential I/O interfere with each other when they share a disk
SQL Server refuses to start if they share a drive
It has no performance effect, only a recoverability one
Log files require more total disk space than data files
questions.explain: The data file's scattered random I/O breaks up the log's sequential write stream if they share a disk, slowing transaction commits.

questions.q: What is the recoverability reason for keeping backups off the data drive?
options: If the data drive fails, backups on the same disk are lost along with the database, defeating the purpose of taking them
Backups take up too much space to share a drive with data
Backups can only be written to network shares, never local disks
It has no bearing on recoverability, only on backup speed
questions.explain: A single disk failure that takes out both the database and its only backup copy defeats the entire point of having backups — this is why the backup drive matters as much as the data and log drives.

questions.q: Why does keeping the log file on a separate, undamaged disk matter after a data-disk failure?
options: It allows a tail-log backup, capturing transactions up to the moment of failure for recovery
It allows the data disk to automatically repair itself
It has no benefit if the data disk has already failed
It only matters if the database is in SIMPLE recovery model
questions.explain: If the log disk survives a data-disk failure, a tail-log backup can capture every committed transaction since the last log backup, minimizing data loss during recovery.

questions.q: According to this lesson, is the recommended drive layout a strict rule to follow exactly?
options: No — it's a starting point; the reasoning behind each separation matters more than memorizing specific drive letters
Yes, every SQL Server installation must use exactly these drive letters
Yes, but only for Standard Edition, not Enterprise
No, disk layout has no real impact on any SQL Server installation
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames the table as a starting point, not a law — a small server might combine some roles, while a large one might split data further, as long as the underlying performance and recoverability reasoning is respected.
